claim: Cytoplasmic lipid droplets are highly dynamic storage organelles that are critical for cellular lipid homeostasis.
source: Cytoplasmic lipid droplets are highly dynamic storage organelles that are critical for cellular lipid homeostasis.
evidence: This is a general statement about lipid droplets that represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Fluorescently tagging perilipin 2 and perilipin 3 in the endogenous loci permits visualization of lipid droplets in the intestine, liver, and adipose tissue.
source: Fluorescently tagging the lipid droplet-associated proteins, perilipin 2 and perilipin 3, in the endogenous loci permits visualization of lipid droplets in the intestine, liver, and adipose tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing fluorescent imaging in these tissues.

claim: Perilipin 3 is rapidly loaded on intestinal lipid droplets following a high-fat meal.
source: Using these tools, we found that perilipin 3 is rapidly loaded on intestinal lipid droplets following a high-fat meal and later replaced by perilipin 2.
evidence: This is supported by time-course imaging data showing Plin3-RFP on lipid droplets as early as 45 minutes after feeding.

claim: Perilipin 3 is later replaced by perilipin 2 on intestinal lipid droplets.
source: Using these tools, we found that perilipin 3 is rapidly loaded on intestinal lipid droplets following a high-fat meal and later replaced by perilipin 2.
evidence: This is supported by time-course data showing the transition from Plin3 to Plin2 on lipid droplets over time.

claim: Lipid droplets are dynamic organelles with roles in cellular lipid homeostasis, protection from lipotoxicity and ER stress, viral and parasitic infection, and host defense.
source: While initially believed to be passive storage depots for lipids, it is now appreciated that lipid droplets are dynamic organelles with roles in cellular lipid homeostasis, protection from lipotoxicity and ER stress, viral and parasitic infection, and host defense (Farese and Walther, 2009; Cloherty et al., 2020; Olzmann and Carvalho, 2019; Roberts and Olzmann, 2020; Bosch et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Lipid droplets were initially believed to be passive storage depots for lipids.
source: While initially believed to be passive storage depots for lipids, it is now appreciated that lipid droplets are dynamic organelles with roles in cellular lipid homeostasis, protection from lipotoxicity and ER stress, viral and parasitic infection, and host defense (Farese and Walther, 2009; Cloherty et al., 2020; Olzmann and Carvalho, 2019; Roberts and Olzmann, 2020; Bosch et al., 2020).
evidence: This represents historical scientific understanding, now known to be incomplete.

claim: Lipid droplets are typically coated by one or more perilipins.
source: Lipid droplets are typically coated by one or more perilipins (PLINs), an evolutionarily related protein family defined by two conserved protein motifs, the N-terminal ~100 amino acid hydrophobic PAT domain followed by a repeating 11-mer helical motif of varying length (Kimmel and Sztalryd, 2016; Lu et al., 2001; Londos et al., 1999; Bussell and Eliezer, 2003; Miura et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Perilipins are an evolutionarily related protein family defined by two conserved protein motifs: the N-terminal ~100 amino acid hydrophobic PAT domain followed by a repeating 11-mer helical motif of varying length.
source: Lipid droplets are typically coated by one or more perilipins (PLINs), an evolutionarily related protein family defined by two conserved protein motifs, the N-terminal ~100 amino acid hydrophobic PAT domain followed by a repeating 11-mer helical motif of varying length (Kimmel and Sztalryd, 2016; Lu et al., 2001; Londos et al., 1999; Bussell and Eliezer, 2003; Miura et al., 2002).
evidence: This structural characterization is supported by multiple citations.

claim: PLINs are recruited to the lipid droplet surface directly from the cytosol, mediated at least in part by the 11-mer repeat regions which fold into amphipathic helices.
source: PLINs are recruited to the lipid droplet surface directly from the cytosol, mediated at least in part by the 11-mer repeat regions which fold into amphipathic helices (Rowe et al., 2016; Bulankina et al., 2009; Ajjaji et al., 2019; McManaman et al., 2003; Garcia et al., 2003; Giménez-Andrés et al., 2021).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: 4-helix bundles located in the C-terminus regulate the affinity and stability of lipid droplet binding.
source: There is also evidence that 4-helix bundles located in the C-terminus regulate the affinity and stability of lipid droplet binding (Ajjaji et al., 2019; Rowe et al., 2016; Hickenbottom et al., 2004; Titus et al., 2021; Chong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: PLINs act to regulate lipid storage by preventing or modulating access of lipid droplets to lipases and lipophagy machinery.
source: PLINs act to regulate lipid storage by preventing or modulating access of lipid droplets to lipases and lipophagy machinery (Sztalryd and Brasaemle, 2017; Granneman et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2011b; Wang et al., 2009; Patel et al., 2014; Granneman et al., 2009; Listenberger et al., 2007; Kaushik and Cuervo, 2015).
evidence: This functional role is supported by multiple citations.

claim: PLINs have been found in species ranging from Dictyostelium to mammals, with more divergent variants in fungi and Caenorhabditis.
source: PLINs have been found in species ranging from Dictyostelium to mammals, with more divergent variants in fungi and Caenorhabditis (Gao et al., 2017; Miura et al., 2002; Wolins et al., 2003; Greenberg et al., 1991; Jiang and Serrero, 1992; Brasaemle et al., 1997; Chughtai et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2001; Sun et al., 2015; Wang and St Leger, 2007; Díaz and Pfeffer, 1998; Yamaguchi et al., 2006).
evidence: This evolutionary distribution is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The human genome contains five PLIN genes, designated PLIN1–5.
source: The human genome contains five PLIN genes, now designated PLIN1–5 (Kimmel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: PLIN1 is predominantly expressed in white and brown adipocytes.
source: PLIN1 is predominantly expressed in white and brown adipoctyes (Greenberg et al., 1991), whereas PLIN2 and PLIN3 are expressed ubiquitously (Brasaemle et al., 1997; Heid et al., 1998; Díaz and Pfeffer, 1998; Wolins et al., 2001).
evidence: This tissue expression pattern is supported by a citation.

claim: PLIN2 and PLIN3 are expressed ubiquitously.
source: PLIN1 is predominantly expressed in white and brown adipoctyes (Greenberg et al., 1991), whereas PLIN2 and PLIN3 are expressed ubiquitously (Brasaemle et al., 1997; Heid et al., 1998; Díaz and Pfeffer, 1998; Wolins et al., 2001).
evidence: This expression pattern is supported by multiple citations.

claim: PLIN4 is found in adipocytes, brain, heart, and skeletal muscle.
source: PLIN4 is found in adipocytes, brain, heart, and skeletal muscle, and PLIN5 is located in fatty acid oxidizing tissues such as heart, brown adipose tissue, and skeletal muscle, as well as in the liver (Dalen et al., 2007; Wolins et al., 2006; Yamaguchi et al., 2006).
evidence: This tissue distribution is supported by citations.

claim: PLIN5 is located in fatty acid oxidizing tissues such as heart, brown adipose tissue, and skeletal muscle, as well as in the liver.
source: PLIN4 is found in adipocytes, brain, heart, and skeletal muscle, and PLIN5 is located in fatty acid oxidizing tissues such as heart, brown adipose tissue, and skeletal muscle, as well as in the liver (Dalen et al., 2007; Wolins et al., 2006; Yamaguchi et al., 2006).
evidence: This tissue distribution is supported by citations.

claim: The genomes of ray fin fish, including zebrafish, have orthologs of human PLIN1, PLIN2, and PLIN3.
source: The genomes of ray fin fish, including zebrafish, have orthologs of human PLIN1, PLIN2, and PLIN3, in addition to the unique PLIN variant, perilipin 6 (Plin6), which targets the surface of pigment-containing carotenoid droplets in skin xanthophores (Granneman et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Zebrafish have a unique PLIN variant, perilipin 6 (Plin6), which targets the surface of pigment-containing carotenoid droplets in skin xanthophores.
source: The genomes of ray fin fish, including zebrafish, have orthologs of human PLIN1, PLIN2, and PLIN3, in addition to the unique PLIN variant, perilipin 6 (Plin6), which targets the surface of pigment-containing carotenoid droplets in skin xanthophores (Granneman et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Fluorescently tagged PLIN reporter proteins are used extensively in cell culture to visualize lipid droplets.
source: While fluorescently tagged PLIN reporter proteins are used extensively in cell culture to visualize lipid droplets (e.g., Miura et al., 2002; Targett-Adams et al., 2003; Kaushik and Cuervo, 2015; Granneman et al., 2017; Chung et al., 2019; Schulze et al., 2020), in vivo lipid droplets have been historically studied in fixed tissues using immunohistochemistry (Frank et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2009), staining with lipid dyes (Oil Red O, Sudan Black, LipidTox), or by electron microscopy (Chughtai et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2010; Marza et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: In vivo lipid droplets have been historically studied in fixed tissues using immunohistochemistry, staining with lipid dyes, or by electron microscopy.
source: While fluorescently tagged PLIN reporter proteins are used extensively in cell culture to visualize lipid droplets (e.g., Miura et al., 2002; Targett-Adams et al., 2003; Kaushik and Cuervo, 2015; Granneman et al., 2017; Chung et al., 2019; Schulze et al., 2020), in vivo lipid droplets have been historically studied in fixed tissues using immunohistochemistry (Frank et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2009), staining with lipid dyes (Oil Red O, Sudan Black, LipidTox), or by electron microscopy (Chughtai et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2010; Marza et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Lipid droplets can be labeled in live organisms with fluorescent lipophilic dyes such as BODIPY and Nile red.
source: Lipid droplets can also be labeled in live organisms with fluorescent lipophilic dyes such as BODIPY (Masedunskas et al., 2017) and Nile red (Minchin and Rawls, 2017a), fed with fluorescently tagged fatty acids (BODIPY or TopFluor), which are synthesized into stored fluorescent triglycerides or cholesterol esters (Carten et al., 2011; Ashrafi et al., 2003; Furlong et al., 1995; Quinlivan et al., 2017), or imaged in the absence of any label using CARS or SRS microscopy (Chughtai et al., 2015; Chien et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Fluorescently tagged fatty acids can be fed to organisms and synthesized into stored fluorescent triglycerides or cholesterol esters.
source: Lipid droplets can also be labeled in live organisms with fluorescent lipophilic dyes such as BODIPY (Masedunskas et al., 2017) and Nile red (Minchin and Rawls, 2017a), fed with fluorescently tagged fatty acids (BODIPY or TopFluor), which are synthesized into stored fluorescent triglycerides or cholesterol esters (Carten et al., 2011; Ashrafi et al., 2003; Furlong et al., 1995; Quinlivan et al., 2017), or imaged in the absence of any label using CARS or SRS microscopy (Chughtai et al., 2015; Chien et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Lipid droplets can be imaged in the absence of any label using CARS or SRS microscopy.
source: Lipid droplets can also be labeled in live organisms with fluorescent lipophilic dyes such as BODIPY (Masedunskas et al., 2017) and Nile red (Minchin and Rawls, 2017a), fed with fluorescently tagged fatty acids (BODIPY or TopFluor), which are synthesized into stored fluorescent triglycerides or cholesterol esters (Carten et al., 2011; Ashrafi et al., 2003; Furlong et al., 1995; Quinlivan et al., 2017), or imaged in the absence of any label using CARS or SRS microscopy (Chughtai et al., 2015; Chien et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Expression of fluorescently tagged lipid droplet-associated proteins in vivo has been primarily limited to yeast, Drosophila, and Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: However, expression of fluorescently tagged lipid droplet-associated proteins in vivo has been primarily limited to yeast (Gao et al., 2017), Drosophila (Grönke et al., 2005; Bi et al., 2012; Beller et al., 2010), and Caenorhabditis elegans (Zhang et al., 2010; Chughtai et al., 2015, Xie et al., 2019), although a transgenic zebrafish Plin2-tdtomato line was recently described (Lumaquin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A transgenic zebrafish Plin2-tdtomato line was recently described.
source: However, expression of fluorescently tagged lipid droplet-associated proteins in vivo has been primarily limited to yeast (Gao et al., 2017), Drosophila (Grönke et al., 2005; Bi et al., 2012; Beller et al., 2010), and Caenorhabditis elegans (Zhang et al., 2010; Chughtai et al., 2015, Xie et al., 2019), although a transgenic zebrafish Plin2-tdtomato line was recently described (Lumaquin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: plin2 is not expressed in any tissues of unfed larvae at 6 days post fertilization.
source: Our data indicate that plin2 is not expressed in any tissues of unfed larvae at 6 days post fertilization (dpf) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Following a high-fat meal, plin2 mRNA expression is strongly induced in the intestine.
source: However, following a high-fat meal, plin2 mRNA expression is strongly induced in the intestine, consistent with findings in mice (Lee et al., 2009) and with our previous RNAseq and qRT-PCR data (Zeituni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Plin3 mRNA is present in the intestines of both unfed and fed larvae.
source: Plin3 mRNA is present in the intestines of both unfed and fed larvae, and the signal in the intestine is stronger in larvae fed a high-fat meal (Figure 1A and B), again consistent with previous data in fish and mice (Zeituni et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The plin3 signal in the intestine is stronger in larvae fed a high-fat meal.
source: Plin3 mRNA is present in the intestines of both unfed and fed larvae, and the signal in the intestine is stronger in larvae fed a high-fat meal (Figure 1A and B), again consistent with previous data in fish and mice (Zeituni et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Neither plin2 nor plin3 mRNA expression was noted in the liver or in other tissues of unfed or high-fat fed zebrafish larvae at 6 dpf.
source: Surprisingly, neither plin2 nor plin3 mRNA expression was noted in the liver or in other tissues of unfed or high-fat fed zebrafish larvae at 6 dpf (Figure 1A and B) as was expected from studies in mouse and human tissues (Brasaemle et al., 1997; Heid et al., 1998; Than et al., 1998; Wolins et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Over-expression of Plin proteins can alter lipid droplet dynamics by altering the rate of lipolysis and lipophagy.
source: We recognized that over-expression of Plin proteins can alter lipid droplet dynamics by altering the rate of lipolysis and lipophagy, which can result in altered levels of cytoplasmic lipid and lipoprotein secretion (Bell et al., 2008; Listenberger et al., 2007; Fukushima et al., 2005; Bosma et al., 2012; McIntosh et al., 2012; Tsai et al., 2017; Magnusson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Over-expression of Plin proteins can result in altered levels of cytoplasmic lipid and lipoprotein secretion.
source: We recognized that over-expression of Plin proteins can alter lipid droplet dynamics by altering the rate of lipolysis and lipophagy, which can result in altered levels of cytoplasmic lipid and lipoprotein secretion (Bell et al., 2008; Listenberger et al., 2007; Fukushima et al., 2005; Bosma et al., 2012; McIntosh et al., 2012; Tsai et al., 2017; Magnusson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: EGFP-Plin2 is only expressed in the intestine of knock-in larvae fed a high-fat meal.
source: Consistent with our whole-mount in situ hybridization data, we observe EGFP-Plin2 only in the intestine of knock-in larvae fed a high-fat meal, whereas Plin3-RFP is detected in the intestine of both unfed and fed larvae (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Plin3-RFP is detected in the intestine of both unfed and fed larvae.
source: Consistent with our whole-mount in situ hybridization data, we observe EGFP-Plin2 only in the intestine of knock-in larvae fed a high-fat meal, whereas Plin3-RFP is detected in the intestine of both unfed and fed larvae (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: No fluorescence is noted in the liver or in other tissues at 6 dpf, regardless of feeding status.
source: No fluorescence is noted in the liver or in other tissues at 6 dpf, regardless of feeding status (for images of whole fish, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data.

claim: The knock-in alleles faithfully recapitulate the endogenous tissue mRNA expression patterns of plin2 and plin3 as revealed by in situ hybridization.
source: Thus, these knock-in alleles faithfully recapitulate the endogenous tissue mRNA expression patterns of plin2 and plin3 as revealed by in situ hybridization of fixed larval zebrafish (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of fluorescence imaging and in situ hybridization data.

claim: Enterocytes are responsible for absorbing and packaging dietary fat, primarily as triacylglycerol, into chylomicrons for export to the tissues of the body or cytoplasmic lipid droplets for storage.
source: Enterocytes, the polarized epithelial cells that line the intestine, are responsible for absorbing and packaging dietary fat, primarily as triacylglycerol, into chylomicrons for export to the tissues of the body or cytoplasmic lipid droplets for storage (Demignot et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: EGFP-Plin2 decorates the surface of BODIPY 558/568-C12-positive lipid droplets in the intestine.
source: As shown in Figure 1G, EGFP-Plin2 decorates the surface of BODIPY 558/568-C12-positive lipid droplets in the intestine, which is visualized as rings of EGFP fluorescence in a single confocal z-plane.
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Plin3-RFP localizes to the surface of intestinal lipid droplets labeled with the green fluorescent BODIPY FL-C12 fatty acid analog.
source: Similarly, Plin3-RFP localizes to the surface of intestinal lipid droplets labeled with the green fluorescent BODIPY FL-C12 fatty acid analog (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Lipid droplets can be labeled by both EGFP-Plin2 and Plin3-RFP proteins.
source: In larvae heterozygous for both Fus(EGFP-plin2) and Fus(plin3-RFP), we found that lipid droplets can be labeled by both EGFP-Plin2 and Plin3-RFP proteins (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: No lipid droplets are found in enterocytes in fasted mice.
source: Lipid droplets in the intestine are very dynamic. No lipid droplets are found in enterocytes in fasted mice, but in the initial hours following a high-fat meal, lipid droplets grow in number and size, and then are nearly depleted 12 hr later (Zhu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In the initial hours following a high-fat meal, lipid droplets grow in number and size in mouse enterocytes, and then are nearly depleted 12 hr later.
source: Lipid droplets in the intestine are very dynamic. No lipid droplets are found in enterocytes in fasted mice, but in the initial hours following a high-fat meal, lipid droplets grow in number and size, and then are nearly depleted 12 hr later (Zhu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: PLIN3 is located on lipid droplets following an acute high-fat meal in mice, but not following chronic high-fat feeding.
source: Prior studies in mice have suggested that PLIN3 is located on lipid droplets following an acute high-fat meal, but not following chronic high-fat feeding (Lee et al., 2009; D'Aquila et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Despite upregulation of PLIN2 protein in the mouse intestine following an acute feed, PLIN2 was only present on lipid droplets in enterocytes following chronic high-fat feeding.
source: In contrast, despite upregulation of PLIN2 protein in the mouse intestine following an acute feed, PLIN2 was only present on lipid droplets in enterocytes following chronic high-fat feeding (Lee et al., 2009; D'Aquila et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Plin3-RFP fluorescence maximally increases approximately twofold, occurring ~14–16 hr after the onset of the meal.
source: The Plin3-RFP fluorescence, which is present in unfed fish, maximally increases approximately twofold, occurring ~14–16 hr after the onset of the meal.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements over time.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of EGFP-Plin2 increases ~20 million-fold, peaking at 8–12 hr.
source: In contrast, the fluorescence intensity of EGFP-Plin2 increases ~20 million-fold, peaking at 8–12 hr.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements over time.

claim: There is substantial variability in the fluorescence intensity of individual Fus(EGFP-plin2)/+ fish at any given time-point.
source: Furthermore, there is substantial variability in the fluorescence intensity of individual Fus(EGFP-plin2)/+ fish at any given time-point (Figure 2C), which can be explained, in part, by differences in the quantity of lipid consumed (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements and correlation with lipid consumption shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Variability in EGFP-Plin2 fluorescence intensity can be explained, in part, by differences in the quantity of lipid consumed.
source: Furthermore, there is substantial variability in the fluorescence intensity of individual Fus(EGFP-plin2)/+ fish at any given time-point (Figure 2C), which can be explained, in part, by differences in the quantity of lipid consumed (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PLIN3 is expressed throughout the cytoplasm in cells in the absence of lipid droplets and binds to nascent lipid droplets as they emerge from the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: PLIN3 is expressed throughout the cytoplasm in cells, including enterocytes, in the absence of lipid droplets and binds to nascent lipid droplets as they emerge from the endoplasmic reticulum (Wolins et al., 2005; Bulankina et al., 2009; Skinner et al., 2009; Chung et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: PLIN2 is only stable when bound to lipid droplets and is quickly ubiquitinated and degraded in the absence of droplets.
source: In contrast, PLIN2 is only stable when bound to lipid droplets and is quickly ubiquitinated and degraded in the absence of droplets (Xu et al., 2005; Takahashi et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2019; Masuda et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: In unfed larval zebrafish, in the absence of lipid droplets, Plin3-RFP is distributed throughout the cytoplasm of the intestinal enterocytes.
source: In keeping with these data, we find that in unfed larval zebrafish, in the absence of lipid droplets, Plin3-RFP is distributed throughout the cytoplasm of the intestinal enterocytes (Figure 3A and B, unfed).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: After consuming a high-fat meal, the Plin3-RFP pattern changes: there is less cytoplasmic signal and bright puncta are present, which likely correspond to clusters of small lipid droplets.
source: After consuming a high-fat meal, the Plin3-RFP pattern changes considerably: there is less cytoplasmic signal and bright puncta are present, which likely correspond to clusters of small lipid droplets (1.5 hr).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data and inference about the identity of the puncta.

claim: Weak EGFP-Plin2 signal, almost exclusively on lipid droplets, only emerges ~2–3 hr after the start of a meal.
source: Conversely, weak EGFP-Plin2 signal, almost exclusively on lipid droplets, only emerges ~2–3 hr after the start of a meal, which is consistent with the need to both transcribe (Figure 1A and Zeituni et al., 2016) and translate the protein after the start of the meal.
evidence: This is supported by time-course imaging data and inference about transcription and translation requirements.

claim: The timing of EGFP-Plin2 appearance is consistent with the need to both transcribe and translate the protein after the start of the meal.
source: Conversely, weak EGFP-Plin2 signal, almost exclusively on lipid droplets, only emerges ~2–3 hr after the start of a meal, which is consistent with the need to both transcribe (Figure 1A and Zeituni et al., 2016) and translate the protein after the start of the meal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of mRNA expression and protein appearance.

claim: As time continues after a meal, the EGFP-Plin2 signal on droplets increases strongly, whereas the Plin3-RFP fluorescence becomes predominantly cytoplasmic again by 6–7 hr.
source: As time continues, the EGFP-Plin2 signal on droplets increases strongly, whereas the Plin3-RFP fluorescence becomes predominantly cytoplasmic again by 6–7 hr.
evidence: This is supported by time-course imaging data.

claim: Within 45 min of meal onset, the green BODIPY FL-C12 is present within the intestinal lumen and throughout the cytoplasm of the enterocytes and is incorporated into lipids stored within nascent lipid droplets.
source: Within 45 min of meal onset, the green BODIPY FL-C12 is present within the intestinal lumen and throughout the cytoplasm of the enterocytes. It is also incorporated into lipids stored within nascent lipid droplets, which appear in puncta that are modestly brighter than the surrounding cytoplasm (Figure 4A, Figure 4—video 1, Figure 4—video 2, Figure 4—video 3).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 4A and videos.

claim: Over the next few hours after feeding, the lipid droplets grow in size and the contrast between the BODIPY signal in the lipid droplet vs. the cytoplasm is enhanced.
source: Over the next few hours, the lipid droplets grow in size and the contrast between the BODIPY signal in the lipid droplet vs. the cytoplasm is enhanced.
evidence: This is supported by time-course imaging data.

claim: In many fish, lipid droplets continue to be present in the enterocytes 30 hr following the onset of the meal, although their numbers are greatly reduced.
source: In many fish, lipid droplets continue to be present in the enterocytes 30 hr following the onset of the meal, although their numbers are greatly reduced.
evidence: This is supported by time-course imaging data.

claim: Plin3-RFP associates with the BODIPY-positive lipid droplet puncta as soon as 45 min after feeding.
source: Consistent with our previous imaging (Figure 3A and B), the Plin3-RFP, which is already present in the cytoplasm in the absence of food, associates with the BODIPY-positive lipid droplet puncta as soon as 45 min (Plin3 on lipid droplets vs. cytoplasm, p < 0.0001; two-way ANOVA with Šídák multiple comparisons test), the first time-point we could reliably image after feeding.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of confocal imaging data with statistical testing.

claim: Plin3 continues to visibly coat lipid droplets for ~6 hr, although the mean fluorescence intensity on the droplets is declining over this time.
source: Plin3 continues to visibly coat lipid droplets for ~6 hr, although the mean fluorescence intensity on the droplets is declining over this time (correlation coefficient, R = –0.3266, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity over time shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Between 16 and 30 hr after feeding, there is no change in Plin3 fluorescence intensity associated with the droplets and it is not significantly different from the Plin3 signal in the cytoplasm.
source: Despite the continued presence of lipid droplets, between 16 and 30 hr, there is no change in Plin3 fluorescence intensity associated with the droplets (R = 0.0349) and it is not significantly different from the Plin3 signal in the cytoplasm (p > 0.99; two-way ANOVA with Šídák multiple comparisons test).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The EGFP-Plin2 signal is first visibly detected in the enterocytes ~2–3 hr after feeding.
source: In contrast, the EGFP-Plin2 signal is first visibly detected in the enterocytes ~2–3 hr.
evidence: This is supported by time-course imaging data.

claim: The EGFP-Plin2 fluorescence associated with lipid droplets increases substantially from 45 min to 8.5 h.
source: While the EGFP-Plin2 fluorescence associated with lipid droplets increases substantially from 45 min to 8.5 h (R = 0.7732, Figure 4D), the first time-point at which it is statistically different from the cytoplasm is at 5.5 hr (p = 0.0103; two-way ANOVA with Šídák multiple comparisons test).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4D with statistical testing.

claim: Plin2 continues to decorate all of the droplets persisting through 30 hr after the onset of the meal, although the fluorescence intensity declines with time from 16 to 30 hr.
source: Plin2 continues to decorate all of the droplets persisting through 30 hr after the onset of the meal, although the fluorescence intensity declines with time from 16 to 30 hr (R = –0.6321).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity over time.

claim: The quantitative analysis of RFP and EGFP fluorescence associated with the lipid droplets vs. in the cytoplasm confirms the progression from Plin3 to Plin2 on the lipid droplet surface over time following a high-fat meal.
source: Thus, the quantitative analysis of RFP and EGFP fluorescence associated with the lipid droplets vs. in the cytoplasm confirms the progression from Plin3 to Plin2 on the lipid droplet surface over time following a high-fat meal (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the quantitative analysis presented in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Over-expressed human EGFP-PLIN2 appears earlier on the lipid droplets than the endogenously expressed EGFP-Plin2.
source: Our finding that over-expressed human EGFP-PLIN2 appears earlier on the lipid droplets than the endogenously expressed EGFP-Plin2 suggests that the sequential targeting of Plin3 followed by Plin2 may simply reflect the relative expression level and affinity of the PLIN proteins in the enterocytes rather than size or maturation of the droplets.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of time-course data between transgenic lines and leads to an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The sequential targeting of Plin3 followed by Plin2 may simply reflect the relative expression level and affinity of the PLIN proteins in the enterocytes rather than size or maturation of the droplets.
source: Our finding that over-expressed human EGFP-PLIN2 appears earlier on the lipid droplets than the endogenously expressed EGFP-Plin2 suggests that the sequential targeting of Plin3 followed by Plin2 may simply reflect the relative expression level and affinity of the PLIN proteins in the enterocytes rather than size or maturation of the droplets.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that over-expressed PLIN2 appears earlier.

claim: The PLIN2 deficient knock-out mouse is less efficient at absorbing dietary fat, has higher fecal lipids, and is associated with an altered microbiome.
source: The PLIN2 deficient knock-out mouse is less efficient at absorbing dietary fat, has higher fecal lipids, and is associated with an altered microbiome, thereby making the knock-out mice resistant to the adverse effects of a high-fat diet (Frank et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.
